# How viruses change

> *An influenza vaccine chosen for one winter can protect poorly in the next, and HIV treated with a
> single drug soon stops responding to it. Both follow from how quickly viral genomes change, and from
> what selects the variants that spread.*

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Learning objectives
- Describe the three routes by which a viral genome changes: mutation, reassortment and
  recombination.
- Explain why RNA viruses and retroviruses accumulate mutations faster than DNA viruses and bacteria.
- Explain how antibodies and antiviral drugs select variants from a large viral population.
- Distinguish antigenic drift from antigenic shift in influenza virus, and explain why shift can cause
  a pandemic.
- Relate viral change to the updating of influenza vaccines and to the combining of drugs in HIV
  infection.
:::

## How a viral genome changes {#sec-vchg-routes}

A virus gains a new trait through a change in its genome, which the virus particles copied from that
genome inherit. The change comes from an error in copying the genome, or from an exchange of genetic
material between two viruses that infect the same cell. The same two kinds of route give bacteria new
traits (see [*How bacteria copy themselves and
change*](../bacteria/bacterial-genetics.qmd#sec-gen-change)).

::: {.concept-tree}
[Routes of change in a viral genome]{.tree-title}

- A new viral genome
  - A change in the genome's own sequence
    - Mutation: copying errors left uncorrected; fastest in RNA viruses and retroviruses
  - Exchange between two viruses infecting one cell
    - Reassortment: whole segments swapped; only viruses with segmented genomes, such as influenza
      virus
    - Recombination: parts of two related genomes joined into one, as in HIV
:::

### Mutation {#sec-vchg-mutation}

A mutation is a change in the genome sequence, and most mutations arise as copying errors (see [*How
bacteria copy themselves and change*](../bacteria/bacterial-genetics.qmd#sec-gen-mutation)). Whether
an error stays in the new genome depends on the enzyme that makes the copy. The DNA polymerases of
human cells and bacteria proofread: they check each base as it is added and remove one that is wrongly
paired, and repair systems correct most of the errors that remain. Most DNA viruses copy their genomes
with DNA polymerases, their own or the host cell's, that also proofread. Hepatitis B virus is an
exception: it copies its DNA genome by way of an RNA copy, with a reverse transcriptase that does not
proofread (see [*Blood-borne and sexually transmitted viruses*](bloodborne-viruses.qmd#sec-bbv-hbv)).

RNA viruses copy their genomes with an RNA polymerase that uses RNA as its template, an enzyme human
cells do not have. The RNA polymerases of most RNA viruses do not proofread, and nothing repairs the
new RNA afterwards. Retroviruses such as HIV copy their RNA genome into DNA with reverse transcriptase
(see [*How viruses are built and copy
themselves*](virus-structure-replication.qmd#sec-vstr-genomes)), which also lacks proofreading. In
both cases the errors stay, so many of the genomes made in one infected cell differ from the genome
that infected it.

| What is copied | Enzyme that copies it | Proofreading | Copying errors left in the genome |
|---|---|---|---|
| DNA of human cells and bacteria | DNA polymerase | Yes | Few |
| Genome of most DNA viruses | DNA polymerase, viral or the host cell's | Yes | Few |
| Genome of hepatitis B virus, a DNA virus copied by way of RNA | Reverse transcriptase | No | Many |
| Genome of an RNA virus, such as influenza virus | Viral RNA polymerase | No | Many |
| Genome of a retrovirus, such as HIV | Reverse transcriptase | No | Many |

::: {.example}
Over years of untreated infection, the HIV in one person becomes a population of many related
variants, which differ from each other and from the virus that began the infection.
:::

### Reassortment {#sec-vchg-reassortment}

Some viruses carry their genome as several separate pieces, a segmented genome; influenza virus has
eight segments of RNA (see [*How viruses are built and copy
themselves*](virus-structure-replication.qmd#sec-vstr-genomes)). When two related viruses with
segmented genomes infect the same cell, each new particle assembled in that cell can package segments
from either parent. **Reassortment** is this exchange: the formation of a new virus that carries a mix
of genome segments from two parent viruses that infected the same cell.

Reassortment makes a large change in one step. A whole gene, such as the gene for haemagglutinin, can
be replaced by a different version from another virus. It requires a segmented genome and a cell
infected by both parents at once.

::: {.example}
In an airway cell infected with two different influenza viruses, the new particles can carry any
combination of the two parents' eight segments, including a haemagglutinin segment from one parent
and the other seven segments from the other.
:::

### Recombination {#sec-vchg-recombination}

**Recombination** is the joining of parts of two related viral genomes into one new genome, in a cell
infected by both. The copying enzyme switches from one template to the other partway through, so the
new genome carries a stretch of each. Recombination does not need a segmented genome.

HIV packages two copies of its RNA genome in each particle. A cell infected by two different HIV
strains can release particles that carry one RNA of each strain. When such a particle infects its next
cell, reverse transcriptase can move between the two RNA templates as it copies them, and the DNA it
makes is a mosaic of both strains.

::: {.example}
A person infected with two HIV strains can produce recombinant viruses that combine genes of both, and
some recombinant HIV strains now spread between people as strains in their own right.
:::

## Selection of variants {#sec-vchg-selection}

Copying errors produce variants at random. Whether a variant becomes common depends on selection, as
it does in bacteria (see [*How bacteria copy themselves and
change*](../bacteria/bacterial-genetics.qmd#sec-gen-mutation)). Viral populations are well placed for
selection to act quickly. An infected person carries a very large number of virus particles, and new
generations are produced continually throughout the infection. With so many genomes copied, a variant
carrying any particular single mutation is likely to be present before a drug or an antibody first
meets the virus.

Most variants are no fitter than the parent virus, and many cannot copy themselves at all. Two
pressures favour the few that differ in a useful way:

- Antibodies, proteins made by the immune system after infection or vaccination that bind a
  particular shape on a microbe, stop virus particles from attaching to cells. A variant whose surface
  protein has changed where antibodies bind escapes them and goes on infecting cells.
- An antiviral drug blocks a viral enzyme, such as reverse transcriptase or neuraminidase. A variant
  whose enzyme has changed where the drug binds goes on copying itself while the parent virus is
  blocked.

::: {.flow}
1. Copying errors make many variants
2. Antibodies or a drug block most of them
3. A variant that escapes keeps multiplying
4. It replaces the original population
5. It spreads to other hosts
:::

As in bacteria, the antibody or the drug does not cause the mutation it selects. The variant existed
before the pressure was applied.

## Drift and shift in influenza {#sec-vchg-influenza}

Haemagglutinin and neuraminidase, the two proteins on the surface of influenza virus (see [*How
viruses are built and copy themselves*](virus-structure-replication.qmd#sec-vstr-structure)), are the
main targets of protective antibodies. They are the virus's main surface antigens, the molecules that
antibodies recognise. They change in two ways, which differ in size and in consequence.

### Antigenic drift {#sec-vchg-drift}

**Antigenic drift** is the gradual change in a virus's surface antigens through the accumulation of
point mutations. In influenza virus, mutations in the haemagglutinin and neuraminidase genes alter a
few amino acids in the regions that antibodies bind. Antibodies left by earlier infection or
vaccination bind the new variants less well, so those variants are selected and spread. Immunity from
earlier years therefore protects only partly, and influenza continues to cause epidemics year after
year.

### Antigenic shift {#sec-vchg-shift}

The haemagglutinins of influenza A viruses fall into distinct subtypes, numbered H1, H2, H3 and so on,
and the neuraminidases into N subtypes. Antibodies against one subtype do not protect against another.
Viruses are named by the pair, such as H1N1 or H3N2. Wild water birds carry influenza A viruses of
many subtypes that do not circulate in people.

**Antigenic shift** is the sudden appearance in human influenza A viruses of a haemagglutinin, often
with a neuraminidase, of a subtype new to the human population, usually acquired by reassortment
between a human influenza virus and an animal influenza virus. Reassortment needs one cell infected by
both viruses. Pigs can be infected by both bird and human influenza viruses, so reassortment can occur
in a pig, or in a person infected with both. Few or no people have antibodies to the new subtype, so
the virus can spread through every age group and across many countries as a pandemic (see
[*Transmission, outbreaks and One Health*](../foundations/transmission-outbreaks.qmd#sec-trans-levels)).

The new segment comes from an animal virus. The passage of a virus from an animal host into people,
**spillover**, is the route by which most new human infections arise (see [*Transmission, outbreaks and
One Health*](../foundations/transmission-outbreaks.qmd#sec-trans-onehealth)).

::: {.example}
The 1968 pandemic virus arose when a human influenza virus acquired a new haemagglutinin segment, H3,
from a bird influenza virus by reassortment; its H3N2 descendants still circulate and change by drift.
:::

<div data-island="contrast-pair" data-src="/diagrams/pair-drift-shift.yml"></div>

## Consequences {#sec-vchg-consequences}

### Vaccines against changing viruses {#sec-vchg-vaccines}

A vaccine produces antibodies against the virus as it was when the vaccine was made (see [*Detecting
and controlling microbes*](../foundations/detection-control.qmd#sec-det-prevent)). For influenza
virus, drift moves the circulating strains away from the vaccine strains each season. Laboratories
therefore track the influenza viruses circulating worldwide, and the strains in the vaccine are
reviewed every year and replaced when drift has made the previous ones a poor match. A virus produced
by shift needs a new vaccine altogether, and making one takes months after the virus appears.

::: {.example}
Measles virus is also an RNA virus whose polymerase lacks proofreading, yet the same measles vaccine
has protected for decades. Its surface proteins have not changed in ways that let it escape the
antibodies the vaccine produces, so rapid mutation makes escape possible without making it certain.
:::

The variation of HIV, within one person and between people, is one reason why no vaccine against HIV
has yet succeeded.

### Resistance to antiviral drugs {#sec-vchg-resistance}

Antiviral drugs block viral enzymes and other viral proteins (see [*Detecting viruses and antiviral
targets*](detecting-viruses.qmd#sec-vdet-targets)). A mutation in the gene for the drug's target can
make the drug bind poorly, and the drug then selects the variant that carries it. Influenza virus, for
example, can become resistant to neuraminidase inhibitors through a mutation in its neuraminidase gene.

HIV becomes resistant quickly when one drug is used alone, because the virus population in an
untreated person is large and copied continually with errors, so variants resistant to any single drug
are likely to exist before treatment starts. HIV infection is therefore treated with a combination of
drugs (see [*Detecting viruses and antiviral targets*](detecting-viruses.qmd#sec-vdet-resistance)).

::: {.example}
When reverse transcriptase inhibitors were first given alone in HIV infection, resistant variants
replaced the original virus in many patients, whereas combinations of drugs keep the virus suppressed
for many years in people who take them consistently.
:::
